You should try the following : check your connection, disable ad-blocker, clear your browser cache, try in private mode, try from another browser/computer/connection. 0 Irish Gauge On each player's turn, they can either place a share of one of five companies up for auction, build track (represented by cubes) in one of these five companies, upgrade a town to a city, or call for dividends. The dividends are paid out to shareholders of certain railroads based on how many cities/towns they connect to and how many shares of this company have been issued. The upgrade and dividend actions also affect game length and the likelihood of further dividends for each company. The game ends when a certain condition is met at the end of a player's turn, and the player with the highest sum of money and stock value at the end of this turn wins. Number of players: 3 - 5 Game duration: 35 mn Complexity: 2 / 5 Play Irish Gauge and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Goal of the game Earn the most money by investing in railway companies and expanding their networks across Ireland. Game flow overview Irish Gauge is played over a series of turns. On your turn, you choose and complete one action from four possible options (see below). The game ends when the last dividend cube is drawn from the bag. Start of the game - initial auction One share of each railroad company is auctioned, starting with Yellow. Taking turns clockwise, players bid on the Share up for auction. The minimum bid is the large printed value on the Share Certificate. Players may pass and if they do they may not re-enter bidding for that share. The winner becomes the starting bidder for the next share. Continue until one share of each company has been purchased; each player may end up with one share, or multiple, or none. Available actions on your turn 1. Auction a share : Choose any available share and make an opening bid, which must be at least the large value printed on the share. Bidding continues as in the initial auction until the share is sold. 2. Build track : Place track in the hexes on the board. You may only build track for companies in which you own shares, and track must extend from existing matching track. You may spend up to 3 build points, where; unoccupied easy terrain (light green hex) costs 1 occupied easy terrain (light green hex) costs 1.5 difficult terrain (dark green hex) costs 2 (only one railway may occupy a difficult terrain hex) unoccupied urban hex costs 1 occupied urban hex costs 1.5 Each time a Railway connects all three of the Major Cities, a special Dividend immediately occurs. Any player who owns a Share of that Railway splits £12. 3. Develop a Town to a City Choose a cube from the bag and place it on an urban hex, to convert it to a city. The town must be connected to a Railway in which you own at least one Share. 4. Call for dividends Draw 3 cubes at random from the bag. The drawn dividend cubes determine which cities pay dividends this turn. A City only pays if at least one of the 3 drawn Dividend cubes is the same colour as the Special Interest cube in the City. Payouts do not happen multiple times if multiple cubes of the same color are drawn. The dividend paid by each company is determined and paid: To generate income and payout to Shareholders, the Railway must: connect to a paying City and a Town, OR connect to two paying Cities. If the Railway meets one or both of these requirements, the Railway generates income: Paying Cities each generate £4. Paying Towns each generate £2. The total company dividend is split between the shareholders. [Rating: 1/10] Game felt like it dragged on forever and since it's not very dynamic, it was just 70 mins of boring. Calculating income every time was also incredibly tedious, and it's one of those games where if you're behind its almost impossible to get caught back up and then you're just playing out the remaining 45 mins knowing full well you can't do anything anymore to change the outcome. Literal torture. Never playing again.

[Rating: 1/10] Emphasizes the parts of train games I don't even find that much fun. The minimalist pieces just get all over each other on the map and make it MORE confusing. There's usually 3 or 4 stocks per company up for bid, yay math.

[Rating: 2/10] Poor man's Wabash Cannonball. I will play another time to check I'm not missing anything but in a world where Wabash exists I don't see much reason to play this.  I felt the lack of null actions or timer control made it very difficult to play from behind or try to adjust incentives to get back into the game after coming out of the auction in a bad situation. Combined with shares having an end-game value, the result was most auctions consisting of a richer player buying the share for [opponent in auction's money]+1.

[Rating: 2/10] A "Ticket to Ride" type game that is much worse than that.  Not well-play-tested and half of the actions do not make strategic sense.  This one goes to "sell it" after two plays.

[Rating: 2/10] Several plays in, there's [i]something[/i] that keeps drawing me back despite a handful of things that squarely land it toward the bottom of cube rails games for me. Alas, having trouble articulating exactly what those things are. Stockholding seems...off? Stocks are worth a preprinted value (no treasuries in the game, mind you) and are worth said printed value for you at the end of the game, which feels both strange and unpleasantly safe. [Rating: 2/10] Very poor game design. Random dividend payouts that can effect the number of payouts over the game due to luck of the draw, bad. Track building is too limited to allow one to change your fortunes if you are behind. The poor stay poor because they can be out bid and they really won't ever be in a situation to make more money. Not sure why I gave it 2 out of 10 instead of 1. Probably because with house rules I could probably save this train wreck.

I don't like how money is paid to the bank, that laying track don't cost money for companies, and that dividends payout is an action. I also found the repeated counting of shifting share dividends a bit tedious, although the dividends track help a lot if you remember to update it. [Rating: 3/10] Cube rails, but it has too much chaos. Checkout Wabash Cannonball/Chicago Express which is the cube rail to beat. + Box cover is lovely, truly beautiful work + Simple rules / easy teach – Repeated calling for dividends can swing game radically – There is a lot of king making in this one

[Rating: 3/10] Had a very odd experience with this game. A player connected two cities with a line only he had invested in while we were all buying other stocks and investing in building out our lines. Starting action 2 or 3, he just did the payout action, and every time he did pulled the cube he needed from the bank and got a $10 payout. He ended the game extremely quickly and won by a large margin. When we reacted by putting up another share of the stock of that line for auction, he had more cash in hand and won the auction himself. As a result we had a 40 min game experience where nothing we did mattered 

[Rating: 3/10] Similar to Chicago Express, this Winsome game has stock dilution. This means that if you buy a stock that someone else has, they pretty much lose half of the income of a stock (for the first share). I hate this mechanic. It pretty much means that this is a game of people hurting specific people--those who got hurt the least tend to win.
